process.title: Call and scheduling
process.body: You tell us the property, roughly when the tank was last pumped and what the house is doing. We give you a price band before we come out and confirm what could move it.

process.title: Locate and open
process.body: We find both access points. If risers are fitted the lids are at grade; if not we probe and hand-dig to the lid, which is the most common reason one job costs more than another.

process.title: Pump and inspect
process.body: Depths measured, then the tank is pumped down completely and backflushed. Both baffles and the effluent filter are inspected while the tank is empty and visible.

process.title: Report and interval
process.body: You get what was in the tank, the condition of the baffles and filter, anything that needs watching, and a pumping interval based on your tank size and household — not a generic three years.

faq.q: How often does a Davidson County septic tank need pumping?
faq.a: Every three to five years for most households, and every two to three where there is a garbage disposal, a larger household or a smaller tank. The interval depends on tank size against daily flow, which is why we measure sludge and scum depth on every visit and give you a number based on your tank rather than a rule of thumb.

faq.q: What makes one pumping job cost more than another?
faq.a: Access, almost always. A tank with risers bringing the lids to grade is quick. A lid buried under eight inches of soil, a deck, or landscaping adds hand-digging, and national cost data puts that surcharge at $50–$200. Tank size is the second factor: a 1,500-gallon tank holds half again what a 1,000-gallon tank does.

faq.q: Do you pump the tank completely or just the liquid?
faq.a: Completely. A liquid-only draw-down leaves the settled sludge that actually threatens your drain field, and it makes the tank look serviced while the problem stays put. We pump liquid, scum and sludge, then backflush.

faq.q: Can you pump if you cannot find the lid?
faq.a: We locate the tank as part of the job — probing from the outlet line and the house's plumbing exit. If the tank has been paved or built over and cannot be reached, we will tell you before any digging starts rather than after.

services.blurb: A step beyond pumping: the tank is emptied, then the walls, baffles and floor are washed down and the hardened scum mat and compacted sludge are broken up and removed.

process.title: Establish what is in there
process.body: Cleaning is the right call when sludge has compacted or a scum mat has hardened. We measure first — if a routine pump-out is genuinely all you need, we say so and charge for that instead.

process.title: Pump down
process.body: The tank is emptied of liquid, scum and sludge exactly as in a standard pump-out, which is the prerequisite for everything that follows.

process.title: Break up and wash down
process.body: Compacted material is broken up and drawn off, then the walls and floor are washed down so the concrete, baffles and filter are visible rather than coated.

process.title: Inspect the clean tank
process.body: A clean tank is the only time you can genuinely assess it. Cracks, spalling, failed baffles and root intrusion all get found here, photographed and reported.

faq.q: What is the difference between septic tank pumping and cleaning?
faq.a: Pumping removes what the hose can draw out — liquid, floating scum and settled sludge. Cleaning adds mechanical break-up of hardened material and a wash-down of the tank interior so the walls and baffles can actually be inspected. Most households need pumping on a cycle and cleaning occasionally, typically every second or third visit.

faq.q: Does my tank need cleaning or just pumping?
faq.a: If you have pumped on schedule and have service records, pumping is almost certainly enough. Cleaning earns its cost when intervals have been missed for years, when a scum mat has hardened, or when you have bought a property with no records and want the tank assessed properly rather than guessed at.

faq.q: Will cleaning fix slow drains on its own?
faq.a: Sometimes — if the cause was a tank so full that solids were carrying to the outlet. If the drain field itself has been damaged by years of solids reaching it, cleaning the tank stops further harm but does not restore the field. We tell you which of the two you are looking at.

faq.q: Do I need to add bacteria or a starter after cleaning?
faq.a: No. A septic tank is repopulated by normal household wastewater within days. Additive products sold for this purpose are not required by Tennessee rules and are not part of our service.

process.title: Call and triage
process.body: We ask what is happening and where. Sewage inside the house, effluent surfacing in the yard, and a sounding alarm are three different urgencies, and the answer changes what you should do in the next ten minutes.

process.title: Stop the loading
process.body: Before we arrive, water use stops — no laundry, no dishwasher, minimal flushing. Almost every backup gets worse because the household keeps sending water to a system that has nowhere to put it.

process.title: Pump down and find the cause
process.body: We pump the tank down to relieve the system, then work out whether you had a full tank, a failed baffle, a blocked inlet, a filter nobody has ever cleaned, or a drain field that has stopped accepting.

process.title: Tell you what you are actually facing
process.body: A pump-out buys time; it is not always the fix. You get a straight answer about whether this recurs next month, and what the repair costs, before we leave.

faq.q: Sewage is backing up into my house right now — what do I do first?
faq.a: Stop all water use immediately: no flushing, laundry, dishwasher or showers. Every gallon you send makes the backup worse. Keep people and pets away from the affected area, do not attempt to plunge it through, and call us. Sewage in living space is a biohazard as well as a plumbing failure.

faq.q: Is effluent surfacing in the yard an emergency?
faq.a: It is urgent. Surfacing effluent means the system is no longer accepting flow, and in Middle Tennessee's fractured limestone it is also a groundwater concern, which is why the state regulates these systems at all. Keep people and pets off it and get the tank pumped down while the cause is diagnosed.

faq.q: Will pumping the tank fix a backup permanently?
faq.a: It depends what caused it. A genuinely overfull tank is fixed by pumping. A failed outlet baffle, a blocked inlet line, a clogged effluent filter or a saturated drain field will all back up again within weeks of a pump-out. We diagnose which you have rather than pumping and leaving.

faq.q: Does homeowners insurance cover a septic backup?
faq.a: Standard policies frequently exclude septic backup unless a specific endorsement was added, though coverage for the resulting damage to living space differs from coverage for the system itself. Document everything before cleanup and check your policy wording — we provide a written service record for the claim either way.

process.title: Records first
process.body: Before we open anything we check what Metro holds — approval date, inspection dates and the bedroom count the system was permitted for. That single record explains a surprising number of failing systems.

process.title: Open and measure
process.body: Both lids come off. Depths are measured against tank capacity, which tells us whether the tank is being serviced adequately for the load it actually carries.

process.title: Assess the mechanicals
process.body: Baffles and effluent filter are where a system fails quietly. A corroded outlet baffle sends solids to the field for years before anything shows at the house.

process.title: Walk the field and report
process.body: The field is walked for the early signs — soft ground, differential growth, faint odour. You get a written report with photographs rather than a verbal all-clear.

faq.q: How many bedrooms is my septic system approved for?
faq.a: Metro Public Health holds that record and will tell you the approval date, inspection dates and permitted bedroom count for an existing residence. It matters more than most owners realise: the system was sized for that number, and Tennessee makes it illegal to advertise a residence for more bedrooms than its septic is approved for.

faq.q: Does my lot have room to replace the system if it fails?
faq.a: Tennessee requires a septic system to sit entirely within its own parcel with specific setbacks, and requires the parcel to retain sufficient area to replace the system should it fail. Properties that fail that second test create serious problems on sale, and Metro notes that on very rare occasions a residence may be condemned. We assess reserve area as part of a full inspection.

faq.q: Is an inspection the same as a pump-out?
faq.a: No. A pump-out empties the tank and includes a baffle check. An inspection is a documented assessment of the whole system — tank structure, mechanicals, field condition and records — producing a written report. Many owners have the tank pumped at the same visit because an empty tank inspects far better than a full one.

faq.q: How long does an inspection take?
faq.a: Around 90 minutes to two hours for a standard residential system, longer where lids are buried or the field is large. Standalone inspections take longer than the baffle check bundled into a routine pump-out, which is why they are priced separately.

process.title: Report in writing
process.body: A photographed written report separating maintenance from repair from genuine deal issues, in language a buyer and an agent can both act on.

faq.q: Is a septic inspection required to sell a house in Tennessee?
faq.a: Tennessee does not universally require the tank to be pumped before a sale, but sellers must disclose known septic details, and a buyer's agent must present the option of a sewer inspection under TREC Rule 1260-2-.37. In practice a proper inspection requires emptying the tank, so the inspection effectively brings the pumping with it.

faq.q: Who pays for the septic inspection, buyer or seller?
faq.a: It is negotiable and varies by contract. Buyers commonly pay because the inspection is theirs to rely on; sellers increasingly pay for one before listing, because finding a failed baffle at your own pace costs far less than renegotiating with a buyer holding an inspection report and a deadline.

faq.q: What if the house is advertised with more bedrooms than the septic is approved for?
faq.a: That is a real problem, not a technicality. In Tennessee it is illegal to advertise a home for more bedrooms than its septic is approved for, and whoever advertises it is liable for misrepresentation. Metro holds the approved bedroom count. We check it as standard, because it is far better found before closing.

faq.q: How fast can you turn a report around?
faq.a: We schedule against your inspection period and provide the written report promptly after the visit. Tell us your closing date when you call and we will confirm whether we can meet it before you book.

process.title: Rule out the cheap causes first
process.body: A failed outlet baffle or a clogged effluent filter produces symptoms that look exactly like a failing field, and costs a fraction to fix. We check those before anyone talks about excavation.

process.title: Take the load off
process.body: The tank is pumped down so the field stops receiving flow, which both relieves the immediate problem and lets us see how the field behaves when it is not being pushed.

process.title: Open the distribution box
process.body: An unlevel or blocked distribution box sends everything to one lateral and drowns it while the rest of the field sits unused. It is common, cheap to correct, and frequently missed.

process.title: Honest repair-or-replace call
process.body: Some fields recover once the cause is removed. Some are finished. You get the assessment with both cost bands, and we will tell you when spending on a repair is throwing money at a field that needs replacing.

faq.q: What does drain field repair cost in Middle Tennessee?
faq.a: Rejuvenation and localised repair typically run $1,000–$5,000, and Nashville-area repair has been reported from $2,000 to above $10,000 depending on severity and access. Full replacement in Tennessee runs $7,000–$15,000 and up. Middle Tennessee fields sit at the larger end of the sizing range because the soils drain slowly, which pushes replacement costs above national averages.

faq.q: Can a failing drain field be repaired instead of replaced?
faq.a: Sometimes. If the cause is a fixable upstream fault — a failed baffle sending solids to the field, an unlevel distribution box, a filter nobody cleaned — removing it and resting the field can restore function. If the soil interface is biomat-sealed across the field after years of solids, repair is deferral rather than a fix, and we will say so.

faq.q: Why do drain fields in Middle Tennessee have to be bigger?
faq.a: Because the soils here drain slowly. Middle Tennessee is karst country — shallow clay loam over fractured limestone — and slow percolation means a given daily flow needs more absorption area. Local drainfields skew to the large end of the sizing range, which raises the cost of replacing one.

faq.q: Does a sinkhole near my field matter?
faq.a: Yes. Fractured limestone lets poorly treated effluent reach groundwater without the filtration a proper soil column provides, and a sinkhole can undermine a field directly. County environmental health offices across Middle Tennessee enforce setbacks from visible solution features for exactly this reason.

process.title: Site walk and capacity check
process.body: We establish how many tanks the site actually has, their capacity, and what the daily flow really is. Commercial systems are frequently sized for an occupancy the building outgrew years ago.

process.title: Schedule around your hours
process.body: Pumping a daycare or a restaurant during operating hours is not workable. We route commercial work to suit the site, which is most of why businesses change provider.

process.title: Pump and document
process.body: Every tank and compartment is pumped and inspected, and you get a written record — because a commercial file with no service documentation is a problem waiting for an inspector.

process.title: Set a real interval
process.body: Interval is set from measured depths against your actual loading. An under-serviced commercial tank sends solids to a field that costs far more to replace than a year of pumping.

faq.q: How often should a commercial septic system be pumped?
faq.a: Far more often than residential, and the interval is driven by flow rather than a calendar. A church used twice a week and a daycare running five days at capacity have completely different requirements from identical tanks. We measure depths against capacity and set the interval from that.

faq.q: Do you service multiple tanks on one site?
faq.a: Yes, and it matters. Commercial sites frequently have multiple or multi-compartment tanks, and servicing only the accessible one leaves the rest loading up. We establish what is actually on the site before quoting.

faq.q: Do you provide documentation for compliance files?
faq.a: Yes. Every commercial visit produces a written service record, and grease work carries a certified hauler manifest. Metro requires manifest use and three-year record retention for grease, and having the paperwork when it is asked for is the entire point.

faq.q: Our system was sized before we expanded — is that a problem?
faq.a: It is a common and serious one. A system permitted for an occupancy you have since exceeded will keep failing regardless of how often it is pumped. We will tell you whether you have a maintenance problem or a capacity problem, because the fixes are very different.

process.title: Identify the unit and the rule that applies
process.body: A small under-sink grease trap and a large in-ground interceptor carry different minimum intervals — 30 days and 90 days respectively. Getting that wrong is the most common compliance failure we see.

process.title: Service on schedule
process.body: The unit is fully pumped, not skimmed. Skimming the floating layer and leaving settled solids is what turns a compliant trap into a failed inspection.

process.title: Measure against the 25% rule
process.body: The binding requirement is not just the calendar: a unit must be cleaned when FOG plus settled solids reach 25% of capacity. We measure, so you find out before an inspector does.

process.title: Manifest and file
process.body: Every service produces a certified hauler manifest. Metro requires manifest use and three-year retention, so the paperwork is the deliverable as much as the clean trap.

faq.q: How often must a grease trap be cleaned in Nashville?
faq.a: Metro Water Services requires grease traps — typically smaller under-sink units — to be serviced at least every 30 days, and grease interceptors, the larger often-underground units, at least every 90 days. Those are minimums, not targets: the binding rule is the 25% threshold below.

faq.q: What is the 25% rule?
faq.a: You are required to have the unit cleaned when the combined volume of FOG and settled solids reaches 25% of the unit's capacity, whichever comes first against the calendar minimum. High-volume kitchens — fried chicken, fish, large quantities of rice or pasta — routinely hit 25% well before the 30 or 90 day mark and need more frequent service.

faq.q: How long do I have to keep grease service records?
faq.a: Three years. Metro Water Services enforces certified hauler manifest use and three-year record retention as part of its FOG program, alongside interceptor installation and routine maintenance requirements. We issue a manifest on every visit so the file builds itself.

faq.q: How often should an under-sink trap be checked?
faq.a: Weekly. Under-sink units should be cleaned weekly, and if yours is more than half full at the weekly check, the cleaning frequency needs to increase. Waiting for the 30-day minimum on a unit that fills in ten days is how kitchens end up with a blocked line mid-service.

process.title: Records before shovels
process.body: Metro holds approval and inspection records for existing residences. Checking those first regularly saves an hour of probing and tells us the tank's era and likely configuration.

process.title: Work from the house out
process.body: The outlet line leaves the house at a known point and runs to the tank. Following that line is faster and far less destructive than searching the yard.

process.title: Probe and expose
process.body: Systematic probing finds the tank edges, then the lids are hand-dug rather than machine-dug. The goal is a found tank and an intact yard.

process.title: Mark it permanently
process.body: We record the location and mark it. If you want the problem gone entirely, risers bring the lids to grade so the next service is a two-minute open rather than an hour of digging.

faq.q: Nobody can find my septic tank lid — what now?
faq.a: Start with Metro's records for the property, which give the approval date and inspection history for an existing residence. Then the tank is found by working outward from where the plumbing leaves the house and probing along the outlet run. On a typical lot this takes well under an hour; buried lids are common and rarely a real obstacle.

faq.q: Will you dig up my yard to find it?
faq.a: No. Probing locates the tank without excavation, and once the lid position is known it is hand-dug. Machine excavation risks cracking a lid or the tank shoulder, which converts a locating job into a repair.

faq.q: Is it cheaper to locate and pump on the same visit?
faq.a: Almost always. Locating is labour, and if we are already on site to pump, that labour is not duplicated. Booking them separately means paying twice for the same trip.

faq.q: How do I stop this happening again?
faq.a: Fit risers. They bring both lids to ground level, permanently, and cost $300–$600. Every subsequent service is faster and cheaper because nobody is digging, which is why risers tend to pay for themselves across two or three pump-outs.

faq.q: Are septic tank risers worth the money?
faq.a: For most Davidson County homes, yes. A riser costs $300–$600 once. Digging a buried lid adds $50–$200 to every pump-out, and you pump every three to five years for the life of the system. Across two or three services the riser has paid for itself, and it makes inspections and emergencies dramatically faster.

faq.q: Can risers be fitted to any tank?
faq.a: Almost all residential concrete tanks accept them. What varies is lid diameter and burial depth, both of which we measure on site. Tanks with damaged shoulders sometimes need repair before a riser can seal properly.

faq.q: Will a riser be an eyesore in the lawn?
faq.a: It finishes at grade with a lid you can mow over. Green lids are standard and disappear into turf within a season. Compared with an annual excavation scar, most owners find it the tidier option.

faq.q: Do risers cause problems with groundwater?
faq.a: Only when badly sealed. A riser sealed properly at the tank collar keeps soil and groundwater out. An unsealed one channels surface water straight into the tank, which raises liquid levels and loads the drain field — which is why the collar seal is the part that matters.

process.title: Access through the outlet
process.body: The filter sits inside the outlet baffle — the side facing the drain field, not the house. That is where we go in, through the outlet riser or rear inspection port.

process.title: Rinse into the tank
process.body: The cartridge is rinsed back into the tank so the captured solids stay where they can be pumped, rather than being washed toward the field.

process.title: Inspect the cartridge
process.body: Filters crack and warp with age. A cartridge that looks intact from above can be split at the base and passing everything through.

process.title: Advise the interval
process.body: Most households need the filter cleaned at every pump-out. Heavy users, garbage disposals and high-occupancy properties need it more often.

faq.q: What is a septic effluent filter and does my tank have one?
faq.a: It is a cartridge that sits inside the outlet baffle, on the drain-field side of the tank, catching fine solids before they reach the field. Tanks installed in recent decades usually have one; many older Davidson County systems, particularly those from the 1970s to 1990s, were never fitted with one at all. We check on every visit.

faq.q: What happens if the filter is never cleaned?
faq.a: It blocks. A blocked filter backs effluent up into the tank and then the house, which is why a backup shortly after a pump-out so often turns out to be a filter nobody touched. The failure is inconvenient but harmless to the system — far better than the alternative, where no filter exists and solids reach the field.

faq.q: My tank has no filter. Should I have one fitted?
faq.a: In most cases yes. Fitting a filter to a tank that lacks one is inexpensive relative to a drain field, and the field is what it protects. On a system already showing field distress it is a sensible part of stopping further damage, though it will not reverse damage already done.

faq.q: How often does the filter need cleaning?
faq.a: At minimum every pump-out, so every three to five years. Households with a garbage disposal, higher occupancy or a smaller tank should have it done more often — and if you have ever had a slow-drain episode that cleared by itself, the filter is the first thing to check.

process.title: Found during pumping
process.body: Baffles are only visible in an empty tank, which is why we inspect them on every pump-out. Almost every baffle repair starts as an incidental finding on a routine visit.

process.title: Establish which one failed
process.body: The inlet baffle protects the tank's settling action; the outlet baffle protects the drain field. An outlet failure is the more expensive problem by a wide margin.

process.title: Replace and secure
process.body: A new baffle is fitted and secured to sound concrete. Where the tank shoulder itself has spalled, that gets repaired first or the new baffle will not hold.

process.title: Assess downstream damage
process.body: If the outlet baffle has been gone for years, the field has been taking solids for years. We tell you what to expect rather than replacing the baffle and calling it solved.

faq.q: How do I know if my baffle has failed?
faq.a: You usually cannot from above ground, which is the problem. Baffles are inside the tank and only visible when it is empty. The indirect signs are drain field distress on a tank that has been pumped on schedule, and solids visibly carrying to the outlet. Direct confirmation requires an internal inspection during a pump-out.

faq.q: Which baffle matters more?
faq.a: The outlet. The inlet baffle directs incoming flow downward so the tank settles properly; the outlet baffle stops the floating scum layer from leaving with the effluent. When the outlet baffle fails, scum and solids run to the drain field, and the field is the part that costs $7,000–$15,000 to replace.

faq.q: Why do concrete baffles corrode?
faq.a: Hydrogen sulphide gas above the waterline converts to sulphuric acid on damp concrete surfaces, eating the baffle and the tank shoulder from the top down. It is a normal ageing process in older concrete tanks, which is exactly why systems installed in Davidson County between the 1970s and 1990s are now reaching the age where it shows.

faq.q: Can a baffle be repaired instead of replaced?
faq.a: Minor spalling can sometimes be repaired. A baffle that is substantially corroded, cracked through or displaced gets replaced — patching it means opening the tank again in a year. Given the cost sits at $150–$600 against the field it protects, replacement is usually the straightforward call.

process.title: Read the ground
process.body: Depressions, swallow holes and rock outcrops tell you where the limestone is close to the surface. On karst lots that map matters more than the tank.

process.title: Service the tank normally
process.body: Pumping and inspection proceed as on any system. A karst lot does not change how a tank is serviced — it changes what happens downstream of it.

process.title: Assess the field against the geology
process.body: A field that never looks wet is not necessarily healthy. On fractured limestone, effluent can leave fast without receiving the soil filtration that treatment depends on.

process.title: Report against setbacks
process.body: County environmental health offices across Middle Tennessee enforce setbacks from visible solution features. You get a written assessment of where your system stands relative to them.

faq.q: Does a sinkhole on my lot threaten my septic system?
faq.a: It can, in two distinct ways. A sinkhole can physically undermine and swallow part of a drain field. More insidiously, fractured limestone lets poorly treated effluent reach groundwater without the filtration a proper soil column provides — so the system appears to work while failing at its actual job. County environmental health offices watch karst features closely and enforce generous setbacks for exactly this reason.

faq.q: My drain field never looks wet. Is that good?
faq.a: Not necessarily. On karst ground, effluent disappearing quickly can mean it is running into fractures rather than percolating through soil. A field that never ponds but sits on shallow soil over fractured rock warrants assessment rather than reassurance.

faq.q: Why are Middle Tennessee drain fields larger?
faq.a: Because the soils drain slowly. Nashville sits in the Central Basin, where limestone dissolves into sinkholes, caves and fractured bedrock, and the soils above are frequently shallow clay loam over rock. Slow percolation means more absorption area is needed for the same daily flow, so local fields skew large — which is also why replacing one here costs more than the national average.

faq.q: Can I even get a system permitted on a karst lot?
faq.a: Often yes, but the design is constrained. Tennessee permitting requires a site evaluation including a soil morphology assessment by a soil scientist, and setbacks from solution features apply. Some lots need advanced treatment or subsurface drip rather than a conventional field. That is a designer and permitting conversation, and we will tell you when you need one.

faq.q: How often should a mobile home septic tank be pumped?
faq.a: More often than the standard three-to-five-year advice, because the tanks are usually smaller. A 500–750 gallon tank serving a full household commonly needs pumping every two to three years, and sometimes annually. The rule is capacity against daily flow, not the type of home — which is why we measure rather than assume.

faq.q: Is a mobile home system different from a regular one?
faq.a: The tank is typically smaller and the lines are often shallower, but it is the same kind of system with the same failure modes. What differs in practice is the interval, and access — skirting and later additions frequently sit over the lids.

faq.q: The skirting is built over the access. What happens?
faq.a: We assess it before starting. Sometimes a panel can be removed and replaced; sometimes access needs opening up properly, which we will quote before doing rather than surprising you with it. Risers fitted afterwards prevent it recurring.

faq.q: Are these systems common around Nashville?
faq.a: Yes, particularly in north Davidson County. Joelton and Whites Creek have significant mobile home stock alongside single-family housing, most of it built between 1970 and 1999, which puts those systems at 25 to 55 years old.

faq.q: How often should a rental property's septic tank be pumped?
faq.a: At least as often as an owner-occupied home on the same tank, and in practice more. Tenants change, household size changes with them, and nobody living in a rental is tracking sludge depth. A fixed interval per property — set from tank capacity and typical occupancy — is the only approach that holds up across tenancies.

faq.q: Who is responsible for septic maintenance, landlord or tenant?
faq.a: That is a matter for your lease, and we are not the ones to interpret it. What we can do is give you a dated written record of every service and the condition of the tank at each visit, which is what makes the question answerable rather than arguable later.

faq.q: Can you service between tenancies?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the ideal window — vacant access, no coordination, and a clean baseline for the incoming tenant. Tell us the turnover date and we will work to it.

faq.q: Can you cover several properties on one schedule?
faq.a: Yes. Multiple properties on septic across Davidson County can run on a single recurring arrangement with one point of contact, which is considerably less administration than booking each one reactively.

process.body: Metro holds the approval record — the bedroom count your system was actually sized and permitted for. Everything else follows from that number.

process.body: A three-bedroom-approved system in a house advertised as sleeping ten is loaded at several times its design flow on a peak weekend. That is a capacity problem, and no pumping schedule fixes it.

faq.q: Is my septic system big enough for a short-term rental?
faq.a: It was sized for a permitted bedroom count, and Metro Public Health will tell you what that number is. If your listing sleeps meaningfully more people than the system was approved for, you are running it above design flow — which shows up first as weekend slow drains and eventually as a drain field that stops accepting. The bedroom count is the number that matters, not the square footage.

faq.q: Can I advertise more guests than my septic is approved for?
faq.a: Tread carefully. In Tennessee it is illegal to advertise a home for more bedrooms than its septic is approved for, and whoever advertises it is liable for misrepresentation. That rule is usually discussed in the context of home sales, but the wording is about advertising, and a short-term rental listing is advertising. Get the permitted count, and take advice before listing above it.

faq.q: How often should an STR septic tank be pumped?
faq.a: Considerably more often than an owner-occupied home — two to four times as often is common at high occupancy. Guest use is also harder on a system than family use: more laundry per night, more simultaneous showers, and wipes and grease that a household would not put down its own drain.

faq.q: My guests overloaded the system — what now?
faq.a: Stop water use, get the tank pumped down, and have the cause diagnosed rather than assuming it was a one-off. Repeated overloading damages the drain field, and a field replacement in Middle Tennessee runs $7,000–$15,000 and up. If the underlying issue is that occupancy exceeds the permitted design, pumping is a holding action, not a solution.

faq.q: How far should a septic drain field be from a well?
faq.a: Tennessee's subsurface sewage disposal rules set minimum separation distances, and they are enforced at permitting. What matters as much as the distance is what lies between: on Middle Tennessee karst, fractured limestone can carry effluent further and faster than the same distance through intact soil. If your system predates current standards, the separation may not meet what would be required today.

faq.q: Can a failing septic system contaminate my well?
faq.a: It is the risk the regulations exist to manage. Fractured limestone lets poorly treated effluent reach groundwater without the filtration a proper soil column provides — which is precisely why Tennessee regulates these systems and why county offices enforce setbacks from solution features. Surfacing effluent on a property with a well should be treated as urgent.

faq.q: Should I test my well water?
faq.a: Periodic testing is sensible for any private well, and particularly worthwhile after any septic failure, surfacing event or system repair. We do not carry out water testing and will not pretend otherwise — but we will tell you when what we have seen on your lot makes testing the sensible next step.

faq.q: Does having a well change how often I pump?
faq.a: It does not change the interval arithmetic, which is still capacity against flow. What it changes is the cost of getting it wrong. A neglected system on a lot with no well risks a drain field; on a lot with a well it risks your drinking water too.
